questions.q: In the classic 12-1 month momentum formulation, why is the most recent month excluded from the lookback?
options: To reduce the amount of data needed
Because the most recent month alone tends to show short-term reversal effects that would contaminate the longer-term momentum signal
Because exchanges don't report data for the most recent month
It's a purely cosmetic convention with no statistical reason
questions.explain: The 12-1 formulation skips the most recent month specifically because very short-term returns tend to reverse, which is a different (mean-reverting) effect than the medium-term momentum effect being measured.

questions.q: What is the characteristic failure mode of a momentum strategy?
options: Gradual, predictable underperformance
A sharp momentum crash — a fast reversal that hits hardest exactly when the strategy is fully invested in whatever just worked
Running out of eligible instruments to trade
Requiring too much historical data to compute
questions.explain: Because momentum strategies are, by construction, fully positioned in recent winners, a sharp reversal (a momentum crash) can erase substantial gains quickly.

questions.q: A rolling z-score mean-reversion signal is defined as (price - rolling_mean) / rolling_std. What does a z-score of +3 suggest the signal should do?
options: Buy more aggressively, since the price is rising fast
Take a short (or fading) position, since the price is far above its recent average and is being bet to revert back down
Ignore the signal entirely
Hold a long position until the price doubles
questions.explain: A large positive z-score means the price is far above its rolling average. A mean-reversion signal fades this by going short (or reducing long exposure), betting on a move back toward the mean.

questions.q: Why is a carry strategy's return generally described as a "compensated risk premium"?
options: Because it requires no risk at all to earn
Because the yield or roll return is largely payment for bearing a risk (such as a rate differential reversing) that most participants prefer to avoid
Because carry strategies are guaranteed by central banks
Because it only applies to government bonds
questions.explain: Carry earns a steady return specifically because it bears a risk — like an interest-rate differential or curve shape reversing — that most market participants are unwilling to hold, and that risk can show up suddenly in a carry crash.

questions.q: Why do professional allocators often blend momentum, mean reversion, and carry rather than picking a single "best" family?
options: Because regulators require diversification across strategy types
Because each family's edge is unconditionally larger when combined mathematically
Because their characteristic failure modes tend not to be triggered by the same events, so blending reduces the chance all positions fail at once
Because backtests always show blends outperforming single strategies
questions.explain: Momentum crashes, mean-reversion regime shifts, and carry crashes tend to be triggered by different kinds of events, so combining the families can reduce the risk of simultaneous failure across a portfolio.
